In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worthy of mention?﴾ They agree that "hal" (هَلْ, "has/have") here, and in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Has there reached you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 1], means "qad" (قَدْ, "indeed/certainly"), as you say: "Have you seen the conduct of so-and-so?", while you already know that he has seen it. And you say: "Have I not admonished you? Have I not given you?", and your intention is to make him acknowledge that you have given and admonished him. It may also come in the sense of denial; you say: "Can anyone do the like of this?" As for its coming in the sense of interrogation, that is obvious. The evidence that it here does not mean interrogation consists of two points:

The first: It is narrated that when As-Siddiq (ṣiddīq, "the truthful one"), may Allah be pleased with him, heard this verse, he said: "Would that it had been completed, so that we would not be tested." Had it been an interrogative, he would not have said "would that it had been completed," because an interrogative is answered only by "no" (لا) or "yes" (نَعَمْ); but when the intended meaning is information, that answer is then appropriate.

The second: Interrogation directed at Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, so it must be understood as information.

The first issue: They differed concerning the man mentioned here. A group of the exegetes said: he means Adam, peace be upon him. Those who held this view said: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the creation of Adam in this verse, then followed it with mention of his offspring in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, which We test﴾.

The second view: the intended "man" is the children of Adam, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop﴾; so "man" is one in both places, and on this reading the arrangement of the verse is better.

The second issue: Regarding "ḥīn" (حِينٌ, "a period"), there are two views:

The first: that it is a portion of a long extended time, and not determined in itself.

The second: that it is determined as forty (years). Whoever says the intended "man" is Adam says: the meaning is that Adam, peace be upon him, remained forty years as clay until the spirit was breathed into him. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he remained as clay for forty years, and forty as ṣalṣāl (dry clay), and forty as ḥamaʾ masnūn (black molded mud), so his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years; during this period he was not a thing worthy of mention. Al-Hasan said: Allah created all things, what is seen and what is not seen, of the beasts of land and sea, in the six days in which He created the heavens

and the earth, and the last thing created was Adam, peace be upon him, and this is His saying: ﴿not a thing worthy of mention﴾. If it is said: clay, ṣalṣāl and black molded mud before the breathing of the spirit into him were not a human, and the verse implies that a period passed over man while he was a human, yet in that period he was not a thing worthy of mention, we answer: when the clay, being shaped in the form of a human and being judged to be one into which the spirit will be breathed and which will become a human, it is correct to call it a human. As for those who say that the human is the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqah), and that it exists before the existence of bodies, the difficulty is removed for them. Know that the purpose of this is to draw attention to the fact that man is created (muḥdath), and whenever that is so, there must be a creator (muḥdith) who is capable.

The third issue: (لَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْئًا مَذْكُورًا, "he was not a thing worthy of mention") its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "man"; as if it were said: "Has there come upon him a period of time not mentioned?" Or it is nominative as a description of "ḥīn," its implied sense being: "Has there come upon man a period in which he was not anything."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 2:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled sperm⁠﻿ — there are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: al-mashj (mixing) in the language means mixing. It is said: mashaja yamshuju mashjan, when he mixed. Al-amshaj means mixed substances (al-akhlat). Ibn al-A'rabi said: its singular is mashij and masheej, and a thing that has been mixed is called masheej, as you say khaleet, and mamshuj, as you say makhlut. Al-Hudhali said:

As if the feathers and the two notches of it were, opposite the blade, pulled by the masheej.

He describes an arrow that has gone far in its shot, so its feathers and notches are stained with a little blood. The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-amshaj is a singular noun and is not pluralized, as evidenced by the fact that it is an adjective of a singular noun, namely His saying: ﴿a drop of mingled sperm⁠﻿. It is also said: nutfah mashij. It is not correct that amshaj is the plural of mashj; rather both are equivalent in the singular. Its parallel is burmah a'shar, meaning broken pieces, and thawb akhlaq, and ard sabasib. Scholars differed about the meaning of the drop being mixed. Most of them hold that it is the mixing of the man's sperm with the woman's sperm, as in His saying: ﴿It comes forth from between the loins and the ribs⁠﻿ (al-Tariq: 7). Ibn Abbas said: it is the mixing of the man's fluid, which is white and thick, and the woman's fluid, which is yellow and thin; they mix, and the child is created from them. Whatever is of sinew, bone and strength is from the man's drop, and whatever is of flesh and blood is from the woman's fluid. Mujahid said: they are the colours of the drop, the man's drop being white and the woman's drop yellow. Abdullah said: its amshaj are its veins. Al-Hasan said: it means a drop mixed with blood, which is menstrual blood; this is because when the woman receives the man's fluid and conceives, her menses are withheld, so the drop mixes with the blood. Qatadah said: the amshaj is that the water and the blood mix first, then it becomes a clot, then it becomes a lump of flesh. In sum, it is an expression for the transition of that body from one attribute to another and from one state to another. Some people said: God Most High placed in the drop mixtures of the natures found in man, of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, and the estimate is: from a drop possessing mixtures, so the modifier is omitted and the sentence is complete. Some scholars said: the better view is that what is meant is the mixing of the man's and woman's drops, because God Most High described the drop as mixed, and when it becomes a clot, no attribute of being a drop remains in it. But this proof does not refute that what is meant is that it is mixed from earth, water, air and heat.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We may test him⁠﻿, there are several issues concerning it:
The first issue: "nabtaliyhi" means "li-nabtaliyahu" (in order that We may test him). This is like a man's saying: "I came to you to fulfil your right," meaning "in order to fulfil your right," and "I came to you seeking a gift from you," meaning "in order to seek a gift from you." Likewise His saying: ﴿nabtaliyhi⁠﻿ means "li-nabtaliya-hu." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and do not bestow favour seeking more⁠﻿ (al-Muddaththir: 6), meaning "in order that you seek more."

The second issue: "nabtaliyhi" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: We created him as ones intending to test him, that is, wishing to test him.

The third issue: there are two views concerning the verse.

One of them: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the meaning is: ﴿So We made him hearing, seeing⁠﻿ in order to test him.

The second view: there is no need for this alteration; the meaning is: We created him from these amshaj not for resurrection, but for trial and testing.

Then He mentioned that He gave him what makes the trial valid, namely hearing and sight, saying: ﴿So We made him hearing, seeing⁠﻿. Hearing and sight are metaphors for understanding and discernment, as God Most High said, relating the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees⁠﻿ (Maryam: 42). Also, "hearing" may mean the obedient, as in the saying "hearing and obeying," and "seeing" may mean the knowing; it is said: "So-and-so is seeing in this matter." Others said: rather, hearing and sight mean the two well-known senses. God Most High singled them out for mention because they are the greatest and noblest of the senses.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way⁠﻿. God Most High informed that after He had composed him and given him the outer and inner senses, He made clear to him the way of guidance and misguidance. There are several issues concerning it:

The first issue: The verse indicates that the giving of the senses is as a precursor to the giving of reason, and the matter is so, because man is created at the beginning of his nature devoid of knowledge of things, but He gave him instruments that help him to acquire those knowledges, namely the outer and inner senses. When he perceives sensible things, he becomes aware of their commonalities and differences, from which sound primary beliefs are derived, such as our knowledge that affirmation and negation cannot both be true together nor both false together, and that the whole is greater than the part. These primary sciences are the instrument of reason, for by their combinations it is possible to reach the discovery of theoretical unknowns. Thus it is established that sense is prior in existence to reason, and for this reason it is said: whoever lacks a sense lacks a knowledge. As for one who says that what is meant by His being hearing and seeing is reason, he says: when He clarified in the first verse that He gave him reason, He clarified in this verse that He gave him reason only to make clear to him the way and to show him what must be done and what must not be done.

The second issue: The way is that which is trodden of the road, so it is permissible that what is meant by "the way" here is the way of good and evil, of salvation and destruction, and the meaning of "guided him" is: We made him know and explained to him the manner of each of them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways⁠﻿ (al-Balad: 10). "The way" may be a generic noun, which is why its form is singular, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss⁠﻿ (al-Asr: 2). It is also permissible that what is meant by "the way" is the way of guidance, because it is the well-known path that absolutely deserves this name; as for the way of error, it is a way only by way of attribution. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, we obeyed our masters and our elders, and they led us astray from the way⁠﻿ (al-Ahzab: 67)? Rather, they led them away from the way of guidance. Whoever holds this view takes the meaning of His saying "guided him" to be "directed him," and when he is directed to the way of truth, he has thereby been alerted to avoid what is other than it; thus the wording indicates both paths in this respect.

The third issue: What is meant by guidance to the way is the creation of proofs, the creation of the guiding reason, the sending of prophets and the sending down of books. It is as if He, Exalted is He, said: I created you for trial, then I gave you everything you need: ﴿so that whoever perishes may perish by clear proof⁠﻿ (al-Anfal: 42). Its meaning is not "We created guidance," as you see that He mentioned the way, saying: ﴿We guided him to the way⁠﻿, meaning: We showed him that.

The fourth issue: al-Farra said: "hadaynahu al-sabil," "wa-ila al-sabil," and "wa-li-l-sabil" are all permissible in the language.

**The statement of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Either grateful or ungrateful﴾. Concerning it there are several issues.**

**First issue: there are several opinions regarding the verse.**

The first: "grateful" or "ungrateful" are two states (ḥālān, circumstantial accusatives) referring to the pronoun in ﴿We guided him to the way﴾. The meaning is: We guided him to the way while he was in the state of being grateful or ungrateful. The point is that everything related to Allah's guidance and direction has been completed, in both states of disbelief and faith.

The second opinion: "grateful" and "ungrateful" are in the accusative by an implied *kāna* (was). The implied sense is: whether he is grateful or whether he is ungrateful.

The third opinion: the meaning is, "We guided him to the way so that he would be either grateful or ungrateful," that is, so that his gratitude would be distinguished from his ingratitude, and his obedience from his disobedience. This is like His saying: ﴿so that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hūd 11:7], His saying: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them, so that Allah would surely know those who are truthful﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 29:3], and His saying: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and are steadfast, and We will test your reports﴾ [Muḥammad 47:31]. Al-Qaffāl said: The figurative usage of this expression according to this interpretation is the saying of one who says, "I have advised you: if you wish, accept it, and if you wish, leave it," meaning: "if you wish." The *fa'* (then) is omitted. Similarly the meaning is: "We guided him to the way, so [he will be] either grateful or ungrateful," with the *fa'* omitted. It may also be that this is in the sense of a threat, meaning: We guided him to the way; so if he wills, let him disbelieve, and if he wills, let him be grateful, for indeed We have prepared for the disbelievers such-and-such, and for the grateful such-and-such. This is like His saying: ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29].

The fourth opinion: they are two circumstantial accusatives referring to "the way," meaning: We made the way known to him, namely, either a grateful way or an ungrateful way. Describing the way as grateful or ungrateful is figurative.

Know that all of these opinions are suitable to the doctrine of the Muʿtazila.

The fifth opinion, which conforms to the doctrine of the People of the Sunna, and which al-Farrāʾ chose, is that *immā* in this verse is like *immā* in His saying: ﴿Either He punishes them or He turns to them in forgiveness﴾ [al-Tawba 9:106]. The implied sense is: ﴿We guided him to the way﴾, then We made him at times ﴿grateful﴾ or at times ﴿ungrateful﴾. This interpretation is reinforced by what is narrated: that Abū al-Simmāl read *ammā* with a fatḥa on the hamza, and the meaning is: as for the grateful, it is by Our grant of success; and as for the ungrateful, it is by Our forsaking them. The Muʿtazila said: this interpretation is false, because after this verse He mentioned the threat to the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire﴾. If the disbelief of the disbeliever were from Allah and by His creation, it would not be permissible for Him to threaten him for it.

[p. 212]

When this interpretation is refuted, it is established that the truth is the first interpretation, namely that He guided all the responsible persons, whether they believed or disbelieved. By this, the claim of the Jabriyya is refuted, that He did not guide the disbeliever to faith. Our scholars answered: When Allah knew of the disbeliever that he would not believe, and then obligated him to believe, He has obligated him to combine knowledge of non-belief with the existence of belief. This is an obligation to combine two contradictory things. If this is not an excuse for the removal of the threat and the warning, it is also permissible that He create disbelief in him, and that would not be an excuse for the removal of the warning. When this is established, it becomes clear that this interpretation is the truth, and that the interpretation fitting the Muʿtazila's doctrine is not true, and by this the Muʿtazila's claim is refuted.

**Second issue:** He, the Exalted, mentioned His blessings upon man, beginning with the mention of the worldly blessings, then after that He mentioned the religious blessings, then He mentioned this division.

Know that it is not possible to explain "grateful" and "ungrateful" as those who are occupied with the act of gratitude and the act of ingratitude, for otherwise the restriction (ḥaṣr) would not be established. Rather, what is meant by "the grateful" is the one who acknowledges and recognizes the obligation of thanking his Creator, and what is meant by "the ungrateful" is the one who does not acknowledge the obligation of thanking Him, either because he denies the Creator, or because although he affirms Him, he denies the obligation of thanking Him. In that case the restriction is established, which is that the responsible person is either grateful or ungrateful.

Know that the Khawārij argued with this verse that there is no intermediate position between the obedient and the disbeliever. They said: because the grateful is the obedient, and the ungrateful is the disbeliever, and Allah has negated an intermediate position, and that requires that every sin be disbelief, and that every sinner be a disbeliever. Know that the explanation we have summarized removes this difficulty, for what is meant by "the grateful" is not the one who is occupied with the act of gratitude, since that is false both by inclusion and by exclusion (ṭardan wa ʿaksan). As for inclusion (ṭard): a Jew may be grateful to his Lord although he is not obedient to his Lord, and a sinner may be grateful to his Lord although he is not obedient to his Lord. As for exclusion (ʿaks): a believer may not be occupied with gratitude or with ingratitude, but rather may be at rest, heedless of both. Thus it is established that "the grateful" cannot be explained by that; rather, "the grateful" must be explained as the one who acknowledges the obligation of gratitude, and "the ungrateful" as the one who does not acknowledge that. In that case the restriction is established, and their objection is entirely dropped. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, shackles, and a blazing fire.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the two groups, He followed them with threat and promise. There are several issues here:

The first issue: al-I‛tidad (preparation) is the preparing of a thing until it is ready and present whenever it is needed, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is what is ready with me.﴾ [Qaf: 23]. As for the chains (salasil), they are used to bind their feet; as for the shackles (aghlal), they are used to bind their hands to their necks; and as for the blaze (sa‛ir), it is the fire that is kindled upon them, so they are set alight and become fuel for it. This is among the most severe kinds of warning and intimidation.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash‛aris) have used this verse as evidence that Hell, with its chains and shackles, is created, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We have prepared﴾ is a report about the past. The judge (al-Qadi) said: since He threatened with it in a definite way, it became as though it already exists. We say: what you have mentioned is an abandonment of the apparent meaning, so one does not turn to it except out of necessity.

The third issue: It has been read as ﴿salasila﴾ with tanwin (nunation), and likewise ﴿qawarira qawarira﴾ [Al-Insan: 15–16]. Some read it without tanwin, pausing with an alif. For the one who reads with tanwin and declines the word (sarf), there are two explanations:

The first: al-Akhfash said: "We have heard from the Arabs the declension of all that is not declined (ghayr munsarif)." He said: "This is the dialect of the poets, because they were compelled to it in poetry, so they declined it, and their tongues became accustomed to that."

The second: these plurals resembled singular nouns, because they said ﴿ṣawahib Yusuf﴾ (the women of Joseph). When they made it a plural like the declined singular forms, they gave it the same ruling and declined it. As for the one who does not decline it, he treated it like His saying: ﴿Surely would have been demolished monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques﴾ [Al-Hajj: 40]. As for adding the alif in pause, it is like its addition in His saying: "al-Zununā" (the poetic lengthening), so this is likened to the unrestricted lengthening in rhyming verse (al-qawafi).

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what He has prepared for the grateful monotheists, saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar) will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾. Al-abrar is the plural of barr, just as al-arbab is the plural of rabb. The discussion of the true meaning of barr has already been given in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. Then He mentioned, among the kinds of their bliss, the description of their drink, saying: ﴿they will drink from a cup﴾, meaning from a vessel containing the drink. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: it means wine (khamr). In the verse there are two questions.

The first question: mixing camphor with a drink does not make it delicious, so what is the reason for mentioning it here? The answer has several aspects.

The first: camphor is the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is like camphor in whiteness, fragrance and coolness, but it does not have its taste or its harm. So the meaning is that this drink will be mixed with the water of this spring.

The second: the fragrance of camphor is an accident (ʿarad), and an accident exists only in a body. So when Allah creates that fragrance in the substance of that drink, that substance is called camphor, even though its taste is pleasant.

The third: what harm is there in Allah, exalted is He, creating camphor in Paradise with a pleasant, delicious taste, stripping from it the harm that it has? Then He, exalted is He, mixes it with that drink, just as He, exalted is He, has stripped from all foods and drinks the harms that accompany them in this world.

The second question: what is the function of "kāna" in His saying: ﴿whose mixture is camphor﴾? The answer: some said that it is superfluous (zāʾidah), and the sense is: from a cup whose mixture is camphor. And it was said: rather, the meaning is that its mixture was camphor in Allah's knowledge and decree.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: If we say that al-Kafur is the name of the river, then "ʿaynan" (a spring) is a substitute (badal) for it. If you wish, you may put it in the accusative in praise (nasb ʿala al-madh), the implied meaning being: "I mean a spring." But if we say that al-Kafur is the name of this thing called by the name al-Kafur, then "ʿaynan" is a substitute for the place (mahall) of "min kasin" (from a cup), with an omitted modifier (mudaf) assumed, as if it were said: "They drink a wine of the wine of a spring." Then the modifier was omitted, and the modified (mudaf ilayhi) was put in its place.

The second issue: In the first verse he said, ﴿They drink from a cup﴾, and here he said, ﴿from which they drink﴾. So there he mentioned "min" (from) and here the "ba" (with/from). The difference is that the cup is the starting point (mabda') of their drinking and its first limit (awwal ghayatihi). As for the spring, with it they mix their drink, so the meaning is: the servants of God drink wine with it, just as you say: "I drank water with honey."

The third issue: His saying, ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾, is general, so it indicates that every servant of God drinks from it. Since the disbelievers by consensus do not drink from it, this shows that the expression "servants of God" is specific to the people of faith. Given this, His saying, ﴿and He is not pleased for His servants with disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar: 7], does not include the disbelievers; rather it is specific to the believers. Thus the sense of the verse becomes: "and He is not pleased for His believing servants with disbelief," so the verse does not indicate that He, exalted is He, does not will the disbelief of the disbeliever.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They make it gush forth abundantly﴾. Its meaning: they make it gush forth wherever they wish from their dwellings, an easy gushing that is not obstructed for them. Know that when He, glorified is He, described the reward of the righteous in the Hereafter, He explained the deeds by which they deserved that reward:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They fulfil the vow﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: To fulfil a thing is to bring it complete. As for the vow (nadhr), Abu Muslim said: The vow is like the promise (wa'd), except that when it comes from the servants it is a vow (nadhr), and when it comes from God, exalted is He, it is a promise (wa'd). In the usage of the Sharia this term is specific to saying: "For God, upon me is such and such of charity," or making it conditional on something one asks from God, exalted is He, such as saying: "If God heals my sick one, or returns my absent one, then upon me is such and such." They differed concerning when this is conditioned on something that is not among the forms of piety, such as when one says: "If so-and-so enters the house, then upon me is such and such." Some people treat it like an oath (yamin), and some treat it as a type of vow (nadhr). Knowing this, we say: the exegetes have several opinions concerning the interpretation of the verse:

The first of them: that what is meant by the vow is only the vow itself. Then al-Asamm said: This is an exaggeration in describing them as being punctilious in performing the obligations, because whoever fulfils what he has made obligatory upon himself is, with respect to what God has made obligatory upon him, even more fulfilling. And this interpretation is in the highest degree of beauty.

The second: What is meant by the vow here is everything that has become obligatory upon him, whether it became obligatory by God's initial imposition or by the accountable person making it obligatory upon himself. Thus faith and all acts of obedience are included, because the vow (nadhr) in meaning is imposition (ijab).

The third: al-Kalbi said: What is meant by the vow is the covenant (ahd) and the pact (aqd). A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], where He called His obligations a covenant, and He said: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], calling them contracts because they bound themselves to them through their belief in faith.

The second issue: This verse indicates the obligation of fulfilling the vow, because He, exalted is He, followed it with ﴿they fear a day﴾, and this requires that they fulfilled the vow only out of fear of the evil of that day. Fear of the evil of that day is not realized unless fulfilling it is obligatory. This is reinforced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not break the oaths after their confirmation﴾ [al-Nahl: 91], and by His saying: ﴿Then let them complete their rites and let them fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. It is possible that this means: let them fulfil the acts of their rites which they bound themselves to.

The third issue: al-Farra' and a group of scholars of meanings said: "kana" in His saying, ﴿its mixture is camphor﴾, is superfluous (za'idah). As for here, "kana" is omitted, and the assumed meaning is: "they used to fulfil the vow." One might say: we have already shown that "kana" in His saying ﴿its mixture was﴾ is not superfluous; and as for this verse, there is no need to assume it, because He, exalted is He, mentioned in the world that the righteous drink, meaning they will drink, since the present-tense form (al-mudari') is shared between the present and the future. Then He said: the cause of that reward which they will find is that they now ﴿fulfil the vow﴾.

[p. 215]

The second type of the righteous deeds that God Most High related about them is His saying: ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾

Know that the complete obedience is not achieved except when the intention is joined with the action. So when He related their action, which is His saying ﴿They fulfil [their vows]﴾, He related their intention, which is His saying ﴿and fear a Day﴾. The verification of this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Actions are only by intentions." By the combination of these two matters, God Most High named them the righteous (al-abrar). In the verse there are questions.

The first question: The conditions of the Resurrection and all its terrors are the act of God, and whatever is an act of God is wisdom and right. What is like that is not evil. So how did God Most High describe it as evil?

(The answer): It is called evil only because it is harmful to the one upon whom it descends and difficult for him, just as illnesses and all disliked matters are called evils.

The second question: What is the meaning of mustatir (widespread)?

(The answer): There are two views on it.

The first: The terror of the Resurrection is severe. Do you not see that the heavens will split and be torn open and become like molten metal, the stars will scatter, the sun and the moon will be wound up, the angels will be terrified, the earth will be changed into another earth, the mountains will be blown away, and the seas will be set ablaze? Since this is so, he added to it only fear of the Resurrection. The first is that he is described with the attributes of its people among the wretched, as in their saying: "Your day is fasting." It is narrated that the disbeliever will be held back until a sweat like tar flows from between his eyes.

The second is that it is likened, in its severity and ferocity, to a frowning lion or to a brave, valiant warrior.

The sixth issue: Al-Zajjaj said: "It has come in the tafsir that qamṭarīr (قَمْطَرِيرًا, "stern, gloomy") means the frowning of the face, so that the space between the two eyes gathers. One of them: these righteous ones may have said these things with their tongues, either in order that this statement would be a prevention for those in need from repaying them with a similar favour or with thanks, because their kindness was done for the sake of God, exalted is He, so there is no sense in rewarding creatures; or in order that this statement would serve as instruction and a reminder of what one who is sincere to God should be like, so that others might follow them in that path.

Second: that they intended that this would be so.

Third: that this may be a declaration and disclosure of their belief and the soundness of their intention, even if they did not say anything. It is related from Mujahid that they did not speak it, but God knew it from them, so He praised them.

The second issue: Know that kindness from another is sometimes for the sake of God, exalted is He, sometimes for other than God, exalted is He, either seeking a reward or seeking praise and commendation, and sometimes for both. This last is shirk (associating partners with God). The first is what is accepted by God, exalted is He, while the remaining two types are rejected. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], and He said: ﴿And what you give in ribā (usury) to increase the wealth of people does not increase with God. But what you give in zakāh, seeking the countenance of God﴾ [al-Rum: 39]. There is no doubt that seeking thanks is of the same kind as reminders and injury. Having known this, we say: when the people said: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾, there remained a possibility that they fed for the sake of God and also for other purposes by way of association, so he negated this possibility with His saying: ﴿We desire from you neither reward nor thanks﴾.

The third issue: al-shukūr and al-kufūr are verbal nouns (maṣdar), like al-shukr and al-kufr, and they follow the pattern of al-dukhūl and al-khurūj (entering and exiting). This is the view of the body of lexicographers. Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make shukūr the plural of shukr and kufūr the plural of kufr, based on His saying: ﴿But the wrongdoers refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Isra: 99], like burd and burūd; and if you wish, it is a single verbal noun carrying the meaning of a plural, like qaʿada quʿūdan and kharaja khurūjan.

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord﴾ may bear two interpretations:

One of them: that our kindness to you is out of fear of the severity of that Day, not out of desire for your repayment.

The second: that we do not desire from you repayment, out of fear of God's punishment for seeking repayment through charity. If it is said: God related of them the fulfilment of vows and attributed that solely to fear of the Resurrection, and when He related of them the feeding, He attributed it to two things: seeking God's pleasure and fear of the Resurrection, so what is the reason for this? We say: fulfilling a vow falls within the very reality of seeking God's pleasure, exalted is He, because the vow is what a person has made obligatory upon himself for the sake of God. Since this is so, he added to it only fear of the Resurrection. As for feeding, it does not fall within the very reality of seeking God's pleasure, so he added to it both seeking God's pleasure and seeking protection from the fear of the Resurrection.

The first is that he is described with the attributes of its people among the wretched, as in their saying: "Your day is fasting." It is narrated that the disbeliever will be held back until a sweat like tar flows from between his eyes.

The second is that it is likened, in its severity and ferocity, to a frowning lion or to a brave, valiant warrior.

The sixth issue: Al-Zajjaj said: "It has come in the tafsir that qamṭarīr (قَمْطَرِيرًا, "stern, gloomy") means the frowning of the face, so that the space between the two eyes gathers. He said: This is permissible in the language. It is said: iqmaṭarrat al-nāqah (اقْمَطَرَّتِ النّاقَةُ), when the she-camel raises her tail, gathers her two hind parts, and throws out her nose." He means that the meaning of iqmaṭarra in the language is "gathered." Al-Kalbi said: qamṭarīran means "severe," and this is the view of al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mubarrad and Ibn Qutayba. They said: yawmun qamṭarīrun and qumāṭir, when a day is difficult and severe, the most severe and longest of days in tribulation. Al-Wahidi said: This is a meaning, but the tafsir is the first.

God Most High says: ﴿So God protected them from the evil of that Day and gave them radiance and happiness.﴾

Know that when God related of them that they performed the acts of obedience for two purposes, seeking God's pleasure and fearing the Resurrection, He explained in this verse that He granted them both of these purposes. As for protection from the terror of the Resurrection, it is what is meant by His words: ﴿So God protected them from the evil of that Day﴾. He called its hardships "evil" as a broadening of meaning, as you know.

Know also that this verse is one of the things that indicate that the hardships of the Hereafter reach only the people of punishment. As for seeking God Most High's pleasure, He gave them, because of it, radiance in the face and happiness in the heart. The explanation of ﴿and He will give them (laqqāhum)﴾ has already passed in His words: ﴿and they will be met therein with greeting﴾ [Al-Furqan: 75], and the explanation of radiance (naḍrah) in His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. The first: the place in which one sits. He described it with His words: ﴿reclining therein on couches﴾, and they are beds within canopied alcoves (ḥijāl). A single couch is not called arīkah unless it is joined with a canopy. Regarding the accusative case (naṣb) of "mutakiʾīn (reclining)" there are two possibilities:

The first: al-Akhfash said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The meaning is: He rewarded them with a garden while they were reclining, just as you say: "He rewarded them with that standing."

The second: al-Akhfash said: It may also be in the accusative for praise (madḥ).

The second [reward] is the dwelling. He described it by His saying: ﴿They will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾, and on this there are two views:

The first: its air is temperate between heat and cold.

The second: that the zamharir (bitter cold, or moon) in the dialect of Tayyi' is the moon. This is how Tha'lab narrated it, and he recited:

The third: that it is a pleasant garden, and God the Exalted described it by His saying: ﴿And its shades drawing near over them﴾. On this verse there are two questions:

The first: What is the reason for the accusative in "wadāniyatan" (and drawing near)? (The answer): al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj mentioned two views concerning it:

The first: it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) coordinated with His saying ﴿reclining﴾, as you say: "In the house is 'Abd Allah, reclining, and the canopies let down over him," since when He said ("over them") He returned to mention of them.

and know that when He, the Exalted, had described their food, their clothing and their dwelling, He then described their drink, and He put ahead of it the description of those vessels from which they drink. So He said: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that were crystal-clear﴾ ﴿crystal-clear of silver, which they have determined in measure﴾. In the verse there are questions:

The first question: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿There will be circulated among them dishes of gold and cups﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71]. The ṣiḥāf (large dishes) are the qiṣā' (bowls), and they are mainly used for eating. So if what they eat from is gold, then what they drink from is more fitting to be gold, because the custom is to be more refined in drinking vessels than in eating vessels. If this verse indicates that their drinking vessels are of gold, then how is it mentioned here that they are of silver? (The answer): there is no contradiction between the two matters. Sometimes they are given drink in this, and sometimes in that.

The second question: What is the difference between the āniyah (vessels) and the akwāb (cups)? (The answer): the people of language said: the akwāb are the kīzān (jugs/cups) that have no handles. It may be that the meaning is that the vessel in which drinking takes place is like a qadah (goblet), and the kūb is that from which it is poured into the vessel, like the ibrīq (ewer).

The third question: What is the meaning of "kānat" (were)? (The answer): it is from "yakūn" in His saying: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], meaning they came into being as crystal-clear vessels by the creating of God, in magnification of that wondrous creation, which combines the two attributes of the two contrasting substances.

The fourth question: How can these cups be of silver and of crystal? (The answer) concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: the origin of crystal in this world is sand, and the origin of the crystal of Paradise is the silver of Paradise. Just as God, the Exalted, is able to turn dense sand into clear glass, so He is able to turn the silver of Paradise into a delicate crystal vessel. The purpose of mentioning this verse is to draw attention to the fact that the ratio of the crystal of Paradise to the crystal of this world is like the ratio of the silver of Paradise to the sand of this world. Just as there is no comparison between these two origins, so there is none between the two crystals in clarity and fineness.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in Paradise except the names." Given that, the perfection of silver lies in its durability, purity and nobility, but it is dense in substance; and the perfection of crystal lies in its transparency and clarity, but it breaks quickly. So the vessels of Paradise are vessels in which there is obtained from silver its durability, purity and nobility of substance, and from crystal its clarity and transparency.

The third: that they are silver but have the clarity of crystal; and it is not unlikely, from the power of God the Exalted, to combine these two attributes.

The fourth: that what is meant by qawārīr in the verse is not glass. The Arabs call whatever is round among the vessels in which drinks are placed, and which is thin and clear, a qārūrah. So the meaning of the verse is: and cups of silver, round, clear, thin.

The fifth question: How is the recitation of (qawārīra qawārīr)? (The answer): they were read without tanwīn on both, with tanwīn on the first, and with tanwīn on both. This tanwīn is a substitute for the alif of ițlāq, because it is a fāṣilah (verse-end). In the second, it is for following the first, because the second is a badal (substitute) of the first, so the badal follows the mubdal (what is substituted). It was also read: "qawārīru min fiḍḍah" with the nominative, meaning: they are qawārīr. And "qaddarūhā" is an attribute of "qawārīra min fiḍḍah."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿qaddarūhā taqdīrā﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: the exegetes said: its meaning is ﴿they determined it in measure﴾ according to the measure of their satisfaction, neither exceeding nor falling short of their drinking, so that it would be most pleasant for their drinking. Rabi' ibn Anas said: those vessels are of the size of a handful, not large so that their weight would be burdensome.

The second issue: the ultimate aim of a man in the vessel from which he drinks is clarity, purity and shape. As for clarity, God the Exalted mentioned it with His saying: ﴿were crystal﴾; as for purity, He mentioned it with His saying: ﴿of silver﴾; and as for shape, He mentioned it with His saying: ﴿they determined it in measure﴾.

The third issue: who is the one who determined this measure? There are two views:

The first: they are the attendants (ṭā'ifūn) indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and there will be circulated among them﴾, for they determined its drink according to the measure of the drinker's satisfaction.

The second: they are the drinkers themselves, because when they desire a quantity of the drink, it comes to them in that quantity.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verses 17–18:

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, described the vessels of their drink, He then mentioned the description of their drink, saying: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾. The Arabs used to like putting ginger in drink, because it produces in it a kind of pungency (al-laddh). Since this was so, Allah described the drink of the people of Paradise with it, and it must be that in goodness it is at the utmost degree. Ibn 'Abbas said: Everything that Allah the Exalted mentioned in the Qur'an of what is in Paradise, there is nothing of it in this world except the name.

The complete discussion here is like what we mentioned in His saying: ﴿whose mixture is camphor﴾.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿a fountain therein called Salsabil﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn al-A'rabi said: I have not heard "salsabil" except in the Qur'an, so no derivation is known for it. Most of the scholars said: It is said: a drink that is salsal, salsal and salsabil, meaning sweet and easy to swallow, and the letter ba' has been added in the construction until the word became five-lettered and indicated the utmost smoothness. Al-Zajjaj said: Salsabil in the language is an attribute of what is at the utmost smoothness. The benefit in mentioning salsabil is that this drink has the taste of ginger but without pungency, because the opposite of pungency is smoothness. They attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, that its meaning is: "Ask for a way (sal sabilan) to it." This is far-fetched, unless it is meant that the phrase of the speaker, "ask for a way," was made a proper name for the fountain, as it was said: Ta'abbata Sharran; and it was named thus because none drinks from it except one who asks for a way to it through righteous deeds.

Second issue: Regarding the accusative case of "ʿaynan" there are two views:

One of them: that it is a substitute (badal) for "zanjabilan."

The second: that it is put in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas).

Third issue: "Salsabilan" is given tanwin because it is the end of a verse (ra's ayah), so it is like His saying: "al-zununa" and "al-sabila," and the explanation of this has already preceded in this surah.

Know that after this, He (exalted is He) mentioned who would serve in those gatherings, saying: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾. The third attribute is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾. Concerning the manner of the comparison there are several aspects:

First: They are likened, in their beauty, the purity of their complexions, and their dispersal throughout their gatherings and dwellings while busy with various kinds of service, to scattered pearls. Had they been in rows, they would have been likened to strung pearls. Do you not see that He (exalted is He) said: ﴿circulate among them﴾? So when they are circulating, they are scattered.

Second: They are likened to fresh pearls when they have been dislodged from their shell, because these are the finest and have the most luster.

Third: al-Qadi said: This is a remarkable comparison, because when pearls are scattered, they appear more beautiful to the eye, since the light of some falls upon others, so it differs from pearls gathered together.

Know that when He (exalted is He) mentioned the details of the states of the people of Paradise, He followed it with what indicates that there are matters higher and greater than this stated measure, so He said: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾. In this there are several issues.

The first issue: Does "ra'ayta" (you see) have an object? On this there are two views.

The first: al-Farra' said: The meaning is "and when you see what is there," and the omission of "ma" is permissible, as He said: ﴿Now your ties have been severed among you﴾ (6:94), meaning "what is among you." al-Zajjaj said: It is not permissible to omit "ma," because "thamma" is a relative clause, and "ma" is its relative pronoun, and it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave the relative clause.

The second: It has no explicit object and no implied object; the purpose of it is that it be general and all-encompassing, as if it were said: "And when you find the sight there." Its meaning is that the sight of the beholder, wherever it falls, is not attached in its perception except to abundant bliss and great dominion. "Thamma" is in the position of an accusative of place, meaning in Paradise.

The second issue: Know that the worldly pleasures are confined to three matters: satisfying desire, carrying out anger, and the imaginary pleasure that is expressed by love of wealth and status. All of these are considered base, for lowly animals may share with man in one of them. Therefore the great dominion that God mentioned here must be different from those contemptible pleasures, and it is nothing other than that one's soul becomes imprinted with the holiness of the angelic realm and adorned with the majesty of the presence of divinity. As for what is according to the principles of the theologians (Mutakallimun), the explanation concerning it is also that it is reward and benefit joined with honor. So He (exalted is He) explained in the preceding verses the details of those benefits, and in this verse He explained the attainment of honor, which is that each one of them will be like a great king. As for the exegetes (mufassirun), among them are those who understood this great dominion to mean that there are benefits there greater than what has been mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas said: No describer can describe its beauty or its goodness. It is said: The lowest-ranking person of the people of Paradise will look over his dominion for a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end just as he sees its nearest. It was also said: It has no cessation. It was also said: Whenever they wish for something, it comes about. Among them are those who understood it to mean honor. al-Kalbi said: It is that a messenger from God comes to the friend of God with honorable gifts of garments, food, drink, and presents, while he is in his dwelling, and asks permission to enter upon him, and no messenger of the Lord of Might from among the honored, purified angels enters upon him except after seeking permission.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Hamzah read ʿāliyahum (عالِيهم) with a sukun on the yā', while the rest read it with a fatḥah on the yā'. As for the first reading, the way to construe it is that ʿāliyahum is a mubtada' (subject), and thiyāb sundus (ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ) is its khabar (predicate), and the meaning is: what is above them of their clothing is garments of fine silk. If it is asked: ʿāliyahum is singular, while thiyāb sundus is plural, and when the mubtada' is singular its khabar cannot be plural? We say: the mubtada', which is his saying (ʿāliyahum), although singular in wording, is plural in meaning. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Scorning [the Revelation], talking nonsense by night﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 67], and ﴿So the last remnant of the people was cut off﴾; it is as though it was made singular in that it was placed in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar).

As for the second reading, namely the fatḥah on the yā', they mention three possibilities for this accusative:

The first: that it is in the accusative as a adverb of place (ẓarf), because since ʿālī (عالي) carries the meaning of fawqa (فوق, "above"), it is treated in this grammatical function as it is, just as His saying ﴿and the caravan was lower than you﴾ [al-Anfal: 42] is likewise. This is the view of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi.

The second: that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Then this also admits of several possibilities:

One of them: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the implied sense is: "and He will grant them radiance and joy, while above them will be garments of fine silk."

The second: the implied sense is: "and He will recompense them for what they endured with a garden and silk, while above them will be garments of fine silk."

The third: the implied sense is: "and boys will circulate among the righteous, while the righteous are above them, wearing garments of fine silk."

The fourth: "You would think them scattered pearls," while above them will be garments of fine silk. On the first three possibilities the garments are the garments of the righteous, and on the fourth possibility the garments are the garments of the boys.

The third possibility regarding the cause of this accusative: the implied sense is: "You see people of bliss and dominion, above them garments of fine silk."

The second issue: Nafi' and ʿĀṣim read khuḍrun wa-istabraqun (خُضْرٌ وإسْتَبْرَقٌ), both in the nominative; al-Kisa'i and Hamzah read both in the genitive; Ibn Kathir read khuḍrin (خُضْرٍ) in the genitive and istabraqun (إسْتَبْرَقٌ) in the nominative; Abu ʿAmr and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmir read khuḍrun in the nominative and istabraqin (إسْتَبْرَقٍ) in the genitive. The summary of the matter is that khuḍran may be read in the genitive or the nominative. As for the nominative, it is when you make it an adjective of thiyab (ثِيابٍ), and this is evident, since it is a plural adjective qualifying a plural noun. As for the genitive, it is when you make it an adjective of sundus, since sundus is intended as a genus, so it carries the meaning of the plural. Al-Akhfash permitted describing a word that is intended as a genus with a plural adjective, as one says: "The yellow dinar and the white dirham ruined people," except that he said it is ugly. The evidence of its ugliness is that the Arabs use a plural that has the form of a singular and treat it as a singular, such as their saying: "a white pebble (ḥaṣan abyaḍ)," and in the Revelation: ﴿from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80] and ﴿the trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20], since they have made the adjectives of this type singular. So the singular that carries the meaning of the plural is more deserving of having its adjective made singular. As for istabraqun, it also admits of both the nominative and the genitive together. As for the nominative, it is when it is intended as a conjunction upon thiyab, as if it were said: "garments of fine silk and brocade." As for the genitive, it is when it is intended as the annexation of the garments to it, as if it were said: "garments of fine silk and brocade," meaning "their garments," so he annexed the garments to the two kinds, as one says: "garments of silk and cotton." The evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade﴾. Know that the realities of this verse have already been discussed in Surat al-Kahf.

The third issue: sundus is the thinner part of brocade (dībāj), and istabraq is the thicker part of it, and all of that falls under the name of silk (ḥarīr). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and their clothing therein is silk﴾. It has been said: those whose clothing this is are the everlasting boys. It has also been said: this is the clothing of the righteous. It seems they wear several layers of garments, so the one that is above them is the best of them, and for this reason He said: ﴿above them﴾. It has also been said: this is part of His saying: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾. The meaning of ﴿above them﴾ is: above their canopies that have been set up over them is garments of fine silk, the meaning being that their canopies are of silk and brocade.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾. Concerning it there are questions:

The first question: He said in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿They will have gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]. So how does He make those bracelets here of silver? (The answer) has three aspects:

The first: there is no contradiction between the two matters; perhaps they are adorned with both kinds, either alternately or together, as women do in this world.

The second: natures differ; a person may find the whiteness of silver more pleasing to him than the yellowness of gold, so God gives each person what his desire is most complete in and his inclination most intense toward.

The third: these silver bracelets are only for the boys who serve, while gold bracelets are for the people.

The second question: a bracelet is only fitting for women, and it is a defect for men, so how does God mention it in the context of encouragement? (The answer): the people of Paradise are beardless youths in their prime, so it is not far-fetched that they be adorned with gold and silver even if they are men. It has also been said: these bracelets of silver and gold are only for the women of the people of Paradise and for the children, and then the masculine form predominated in the wording. There is another aspect in the verse, namely that the instrument of most actions is the hand, and those actions and striving are what is used to attain the divine knowledge and the lights of the Eternal Presence, so those actions are like the gold and silver by means of which objectives are attained. Since those actions proceed from the hand, those actions are like the bracelet of gold and silver, so the actions and striving are called the bracelet of gold and silver, and He expressed those overflowing lights from the Eternal Presence by His saying: ﴿and their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾. In sum, His saying ﴿and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ is an allusion to His saying: ﴿And those who strive in Us﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 69], and His saying ﴿and their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ is an allusion to His saying: ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 69]. This is a possibility that came to mind, and God knows best what He intends.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾. The word ṭahūr (طَهُور) in it has two views:

The first: intensification of its being pure. Then on this interpretation there are possibilities:

One of them: that it is not impure like the wine of this world.

The second: intensification of distance from filthy things, meaning what hands full of dirt have touched and what unclean feet have trodden upon.

The third: that it does not turn into impurity, because it exudes a sweat from their bodies that has a scent like musk.

The second view regarding ṭahūr: that it is purifying. On this interpretation too there are two possibilities in the verse:

One of them: Muqatil said: it is a spring of water at the gate of Paradise, gushing from the trunk of a tree; whoever drinks from it, God removes from his heart whatever rancor, deceit and envy it contained, and what was in his stomach of filth and harm.

The second: Abu Qilabah said: they are brought food and drink, and when that is over they are brought the pure drink, and they drink it, and their insides are purified by it, and a sweat exudes from their skins like the scent of musk. On these two views the ṭahūr is purifying, because it purifies their inner selves from blameworthy character traits and harmful things. If it is asked: is His saying ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink﴾ the very same as what He mentioned before, that they drink from the spring of camphor, ginger and salsabil, or is this another kind? We say: rather, this is another kind, and several things indicate it:

One of them: avoiding repetition.

The second: He, may He be exalted, attributed this drink to Himself, saying ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink﴾, and that indicates a distinction in this over others.

The third: what we have narrated, that food and drinks are presented to them, and when they finish with them they are brought the pure drink and they drink it, so it purifies their insides and a sweat exudes from their skins like the scent of musk. This indicates that this drink is different from those drinks. Moreover, this drink digests all other drinks, and beyond this digestion it has a wondrous effect, namely that it turns all other foods and drinks into a sweat from which a scent like musk wafts. All of this indicates difference.

The fourth: the spirit is from the world of the angels, and the lights that overflow from the essences of the greatest angels and their chiefs upon these spirits are likened to sweet water that removes thirst and strengthens the body. Just as springs differ in clarity, abundance and strength, so too the fountains of the higher lights differ. Some of them are camphorous, of the nature of cold and dryness, and their possessor in this world is in the station of fear, weeping and contraction. Some are ginger-like, of the nature of heat and dryness, and the possessor of this state pays little attention to anything other than God, the Exalted, and cares little for bodies and corporeal things. Then the human spirit does not cease moving from one spring to another, and from one light to another. There is no doubt that causes and effects are finite in their ascent toward the Necessary Existent, who is the Absolute Light, may His majesty be exalted and His perfection be mighty. When it reaches that station and drinks from that drink, those earlier drinks are digested, indeed they perish, because the light of all other than God vanishes in the face of the light of God and His grandeur and majesty. That is the final journey of the sincere ones (ṣiddīqīn) and the utmost of their degrees in ascent and perfection. For this reason God, may He be exalted, concluded the mention of the reward of the righteous with His saying: ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink a pure drink﴾.

Know that when Exalted God had finished describing the condition of the blessed (al-su'ada'), He said: ﴿Indeed, this has been a reward for you, and your striving has been appreciated.﴾

Know that the verse has two interpretations.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is that it will be said to the people of Paradise, after their entry into it and their witnessing of its bliss: "Indeed, this has been a reward for you, which God, Exalted, has prepared for you until this time. It is all yours because of your deeds, despite the smallness of your deeds." Just as He said, relating about the angels, that they say to the people of Paradise: ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24], and He said: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you did in the days gone by﴾ [al-Haqqah: 24]. The purpose of mentioning this statement is to increase their joy, for it is said to the one who is punished: "This is because of your evil deed," so his grief and the pain of his heart increase; and it is said to the one who is rewarded: "This is because of your obedience," so that becomes a congratulation to him and an increase in his joy. The one who holds this interpretation treats the speech as implied, i.e., "And it will be said to them this statement."

The second interpretation: That this is a declaration from God, Exalted, to His servants in this world. As if He, Exalted, explained the answer of the people of Paradise: that this was, in My knowledge and decree, a reward for you, O assembly of My servants; I created it for you, and I prepared it for your sake. Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: If the act of the servant is a creation of God, how is it conceivable that the act of God be a reward for the act of God?

(The answer): The "jaza'" (reward) is that which suffices, and that does not contradict its being an act of God, Exalted.

The second question: That the striving of the servant be "appreciated" (mashkur) by God requires that God be "grateful" (shakir) to him.

(The answer): God, Exalted, being grateful to the servant is impossible except in a figurative sense (ʿala wajh al-majaz), and it is of three aspects:

The first: al-Qadi said: Reward corresponds to their deeds, just as gratitude corresponds to blessings.

The second: al-Qaffal said: It is well known in people's speech that they say of one who is content with little and praises it: "He is shakur (grateful)." So it is possible that God's gratitude to His servants is His being pleased with them for a small amount of acts of obedience, and His giving them, in return for it, a great reward.

The third aspect: The utmost rank of the servant is that he be content with his Lord and be pleasing to his Lord, as He said: ﴿O soul at rest, return to your Lord, content and pleasing [to Him]﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–28]. And its being content with its Lord is of lower rank than its being pleasing to its Lord. So His saying: ﴿Indeed, this has been a reward for you﴾ is an indication of the matter by which the soul becomes content with its Lord, and His saying: ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾ is an indication of its being pleasing to its Lord. Since this state is the highest of stations and the last of ranks, the sealing (al-khatm) fell upon it in the mention of the levels of the states of the righteous (al-abrar) and the truthful (al-siddiqin).

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 23:

**"Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Quran in stages."**

Know that at the beginning of the surah, He (glorified is He) explained that man came into existence after non-existence, by His saying: **"Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worthy of mention?"** (al-Insan: 1). Then He explained that He created him from a drop of mingled fluid, and what is meant by it is either that he was created from the four elements, or from the four humours, or from the water of the man and the woman, or from the organs and the spirits, or from the body and the soul, or from successive states upon that body, such as his being a drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones. And in whichever of these senses this verse is understood, it indicates that there must be a Creator who chooses, may His majesty be exalted and His greatness be magnified.

Then He explained after that that I did not create him as something wasted, idle and vain, but I created him for the sake of trial and examination, and to this He alludes by His saying: **"We test him"** (al-Insan: 2). Here is the place of the great dispute between the people of compulsion (al-jabr) and predestination (al-qadar). Then He (exalted is He) mentioned that I gave him everything he needs at the time of trial and examination, namely hearing, sight and intellect, and to this He alludes by His saying: **"So We made him hearing and seeing"** (al-Insan: 2). And since the intellect is the most noble of the matters needed in this domain, He singled it out from hearing and sight, so He said: **"Indeed, We guided him to the way"** (al-Insan: 3). Then He explained that, after these states, creation became of two kinds: among them is the grateful, and among them is the ungrateful. This division is by their own choice, as the Qadariyyah (those who affirm human free will) interpret it, or it is from Allah, as the Jabriyyah (determinists) interpret it. Then He (exalted is He) mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers briefly, and then after that He mentioned the reward of the obedient in detail, and this extends to His saying: **"and your striving has been thankfully accepted"** (al-Insan: 22).

Know that brevity in mentioning punishment together with elaboration in explaining reward indicates that the side of mercy is predominant and stronger. From what we have explained, it becomes clear that the surah, from its beginning up to this point, is concerned with explaining the conditions of the Hereafter. Then He (exalted is He) began after that with the conditions of this world, and He placed the explanation of the conditions of the obedient before the explanation of the conditions of the rebellious. As for the obedient, they are the Messenger and his community, and the Messenger is the head and the leader, which is why the address was specifically directed to the Messenger.

Know that address is either a prohibition or a command. Then, before He entered into what concerns the Messenger regarding prohibition and command, He (exalted is He) placed an introduction to strengthen the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) and to remove grief and loneliness from his mind. He did this because occupation with obedience and carrying out the duty of obligation is not complete except with a heart at ease. After this introduction He mentioned His prohibition concerning some matters, and after finishing with the prohibition He mentioned His command concerning some matters. He placed the prohibition before the command because averting harm is more important than bringing benefit, and removing what is not fitting takes precedence over attaining what is fitting. Then He (exalted is He) mentioned after that the conditions of the rebellious and the disbelievers, as will come with detailed explanation. Whoever reflects on what we have mentioned will know that this surah has been arranged in the best of orders and systems. So praise be to Allah, who illuminated the intellect of this weak, humble servant with these lights, and to Him is thanks for it forever and ever.

Let us return to the tafsir (exegesis) and say: As for that introduction, it is His (exalted is He) saying: **"Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Quran in stages."** Know that the purpose of this verse is to affirm the Messenger and to ease his heart regarding what they attributed to him of soothsaying and sorcery. So Allah (exalted is He) mentioned that this is revelation from Allah. Therefore, He emphasised and repeated the pronoun after making it a noun, because emphasis upon emphasis is more eloquent, as if He (exalted is He) were saying: If these disbelievers say that this is soothsaying, then I, Allah, the True King, say emphatically and with exaggeration: this is true revelation and a truthful sending down from Me. This has two benefits:

The first: removing the loneliness mentioned earlier, which arose from the slander of those disbelievers; for although some ignorant people slandered him, the Compeller of the heavens magnified him and confirmed him.

The second: strengthening him to bear the obligation to come; this is because the disbelievers were exaggerating in harming him, and he wanted to fight them. When Allah (exalted is He) commanded him to be patient with that harm and to abandon fighting, and this was difficult for him, He said to him: **"Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Quran in stages."** It is as if He said to him: I have not sent down this Quran to you in parts, in stages, except for a far-reaching wisdom that requires assigning each thing to a specific time. That wisdom required delaying the permission to fight, so be patient for the decision of your Lord, which proceeds from pure wisdom, free from defect, futility and falsehood. Then, when He (exalted is He) had presented this introduction, He mentioned the prohibition, saying (exalted is He): **"So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one."**

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verse 24:

Then the meaning may be: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾ regarding the delay in permission to fight. Its parallel is ﴿Be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges﴾ [al-A'raf: 87]. The second question: He, peace be upon him, never obeyed any of them, so what is the benefit of this prohibition? The second opinion: that what is meant by His words ﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ up to the end of the verse is not the prayer; rather, what is meant is glorification (tasbih), which is speech and belief, and the intent is that he should remember God at all times, by night and by day, with his heart and his tongue. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 76, verses 27–28:**

Know that when He, exalted is He, addressed His Messenger with honour, prohibition and command, He turned to describe the state of the disbelievers and the rebellious. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, these love the fleeting life and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾ The meaning is that what drove these disbelievers to disbelief, to turning away and to disregarding what would benefit them in the Hereafter, is not doubt (shubhah), such that they might benefit from the proofs mentioned at the beginning of this surah. Rather, it is desire and love for these fleeting pleasures and worldly comforts. There are two questions regarding the verse.

The first question: Why did He say "behind them" (warā'ahum) and not "before them" (quddāmahum)? (The answer) is from several aspects:

The first: Since they did not pay attention to it and turned away from it, it is as if they had put it behind their backs.

The second: The meaning is "and leave behind them the benefits of a heavy Day," so the genitive (muḍāf) has been omitted.

The third: "Warā'" is used in the sense of "before," as in His saying: ﴿Behind him is Hell﴾ [Ibrahim: 16], and ﴿and there was behind them a king﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].

The second question: What is the reason for describing the Day of Resurrection as a "heavy Day"? (The answer) is that heaviness is metaphorically borrowed to express its severity and terror, from a heavy thing that wearies the one who carries it. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Heavy it is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned that what calls them to this disbelief is love of the fleeting, He said: ﴿We created them and strengthened their frames, and when We will, We replace their likenesses with a complete replacement.﴾

The meaning is that their love for the fleeting life obligates them to obey God, both out of desire and out of fear. As for desire: He is the one who created them, gave them sound limbs by which they can benefit from fleeting pleasures, and created everything through which benefit can be obtained. So when they love the fleeting pleasures, and those pleasures are attained only when the one who benefits and the thing benefited from both exist, and these two exist only by God's bringing them into being and creating them, this is something that obligates them to submit to God and to His commands, and to abandon rebellion and turning away. As for fear: He is able to cause them to die, able to strip them of blessing, and able to cast them into every trial and calamity. Therefore, in order to secure these fleeting pleasures, it is obligatory upon them to submit to God and abandon this rebellion.

The summary of the discourse is: it is as if it were said to them: Suppose that your love for these fleeting pleasures is a commendable course; nevertheless, that love obligates you to faith in God and submission to Him. So if you were to use it as a means toward disbelief in God and turning away from His judgment, you would indeed have rebelled. This is a good arrangement of question and answer, and a subtle method.

There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: The lexicographers said: *al-asr* is binding and fastening; from it comes "the man was *usira*" when he was bound with rawhide, and "a horse of firm build" (*faras ma'sūr al-khalq*) and "a horse firmly fastened at the hock" (*faras ma'sūr bi-l-'aqib*). The meaning is: We strengthened the joining of their limbs to one another, and the securing of their joints with sinews.

The second issue: "And when We will, We replace their likenesses" means: when We will, We destroy them and bring others like them, making them a replacement for them. It is like His saying: ﴿that We may replace your likenesses﴾. The purpose of this is to show complete independence from them, as if it were said: We have no need at all of any of the created beings; and even if need were assumed, there is no need for these peoples, for We are able to annihilate them and to bring into being their like. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away, O people, and bring others; and God is ever capable of that﴾ [al-Nisa': 133], and His saying: ﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation. And that is not difficult for God﴾ [Ibrahim: 20]. Then it was said: "We replace their likenesses," meaning in creation, even if they are the opposites of them in action. And it was said: their likenesses in disbelief.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said regarding His saying ﴿and when We will﴾ that its proper form should be with "an" (if/that) and not with "idha" (when), as in His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38], and ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾. Know that this statement is, as it were, a criticism of the wording of the Qur'an, and it is weak. This is because each of "in" and "idha" is a conditional particle, except that the particle "in" is not used for something whose occurrence is known; one does not say "if the sun rises, I will honour you." But the particle "idha" is used for something whose occurrence is known; you say: "I will come to you when the sun rises." Here, since God, exalted is He, knows that a time will come in which He will replace those disbelievers with their likenesses in creation and their opposites in obedience, it is therefore correct to use the particle "idha."
