Know that when Exalted God had explained the states of the happy and the states of the wretched, He said after that: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills takes to his Lord a way.﴾ ﴿And you will not will except that God wills.﴾ The meaning is that this surah, with the wondrous arrangement and far-reaching coherence it contains, and with its promise and threat, and its encouragement and warning, is a reminder for those who reflect and an insight for those who seek insight. So whoever wills the good choice for himself in this world and the Hereafter takes to his Lord a way. Taking a way to God is an expression for drawing near to Him.

Know that this verse is among the verses in which the waves of compulsion (jabr) and divine decree (qadar) clash. The Qadari holds fast to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾ and says: this is the plain statement of my doctrine. Its parallel is: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. The Jabari says: when this verse is joined to the verse that follows it, there emerges from it the plain statement of the doctrine of compulsion. That is because His saying: ﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾ requires that the servant's will, whenever it is pure, necessitates the act, and His saying after that: ﴿And you will not will except that God wills﴾ requires that God's will necessitates the servant's will, and the necessitator of a necessitator is a necessitator. Thus God's will necessitates the servant's act, and that is compulsion. Likewise the argument for compulsion from His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, because this verse too requires that will necessitate the act. Then the explanation is as previously stated.

Know that the argument in this form which we have summarized is not subject to the objection of al-Qadi. Nevertheless, we mention it and point out the weakness in it. al-Qadi said: What is mentioned in this verse is taking a way to God, and we grant that God has willed it, since He has commanded it, so He must have willed it. This does not require that one say: the servant wills only what God has willed absolutely, since what is meant by that is the specific matter which it is established that He has willed and desired.

Know that this statement which al-Qadi mentioned has no connection with the argument in the form we have mentioned. Furthermore, the upshot of what al-Qadi mentioned is restricting this general statement to the case that was mentioned before this verse, and that is weak, because the particularity of what precedes the verse does not require restricting this general statement to it, given the possibility that the ruling in this verse is stated in a way that encompasses that case and all other cases.

There remains a question in the verse concerning its grammatical analysis (i'rab), namely: what is the position (mahall) of "an yashaa Allah" [أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ]? Its answer: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and its underlying sense is: "except at the time of God's willing." Likewise is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "illa ma sha'a Allah" [إلّا ما شاءَ اللَّهُ], because "ma" with the verb is like "an" with it. It is also read: "yashaauna" [يَشاءُونَ] with the ya' (third person plural), i.e., "they will".

Thus there emerges from the end of this surah nothing but Allah, and nothing that is from other than Allah. That is the absolute Tawhid (tawhid mutlaq), which is the final journey of the sincere ones (siddiqin) and the furthest point of their ascent through the spheres of divine knowledge. This is because if entitlement were established, then its abandonment would lead to ignorance and need, both of which are impossible for Allah. What leads to the impossible is itself impossible, so its abandonment is impossible; therefore its existence is rationally necessary and its non-existence rationally impossible. What is so is not at all contingent upon will. Furthermore, if a man owes a debt to another person and pays that debt to its rightful claimant, it is not said that he paid that amount to him by way of mercy and favour.

This is because His saying: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills﴾ indicates that everything that proceeds from the servant is by the will of Allah, and His saying: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment﴾ indicates that entry into Paradise and Hellfire is only by the will of Allah. Thus there emerges from the end of this surah nothing but Allah, and nothing that is from other than Allah. That is the absolute Tawhid (tawhid mutlaq), which is the final journey of the sincere ones (siddiqin) and the furthest point of their ascent through the spheres of divine knowledge. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: His saying: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾. If we interpret mercy as faith, then the verse is explicit that faith is from Allah. If we interpret it as Paradise, then entry into Paradise is by the will of Allah, His grace and His beneficence, not by way of entitlement. This is because if entitlement were established, then its abandonment would lead to ignorance and need, both of which are impossible for Allah. What leads to the impossible is itself impossible, so its abandonment is impossible; therefore its existence is rationally necessary and its non-existence rationally impossible. What is so is not at all contingent upon will. Furthermore, if a man owes a debt to another person and pays that debt to its rightful claimant, it is not said that he paid that amount to him by way of mercy and favour.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment﴾ indicates that the pen has dried over what is to occur; for the meaning of "prepared" (a'adda) is that He knew that, decreed it, informed of it, and wrote it in the Preserved Tablet, and it is known that change in these matters is impossible. So the matter is as we have explained and stated.

The third issue: Al-Zajjaj said: the accusative of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin) is because before it there is a accusative noun, and the meaning is: He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and He punishes the wrongdoers. His saying: ﴿He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ serves as an explanation of that implied verb. ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr recited: "wa'l-zalimuna" (nominative), but this is not a preferred reading, because it is conjoined to "He admits whom He wills," and conjoining a nominal clause to a verbal clause is not good. As for His saying in "Ha Mim ʿAsaqa": ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and the wrongdoers﴾, it is nominative because no verb is mentioned after it that would govern it in meaning in the accusative, so it could not be conjoined to the accusative before it; it is therefore nominative by inception (al-ibtida'). Here, His saying: ﴿He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ indicates that implied governing verb, so the difference becomes clear. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best what is correct; and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
